subject: Computer Networking
title: DMARC — Policy Enforcement
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on DMARC — Policy Enforcement.

hook.text: SPF and DKIM detect fakes. DMARC tells the receiver what to do about them: nothing, quarantine, or reject.

buildup.text: DMARC — Domain-based Message Authentication — links SPF and DKIM results to the visible From address.

discovery.text: A DMARC DNS record sets policy: p=none (monitor), p=quarantine (spam folder), or p=reject (block).

twist.text: DMARC sends reports back to domain owners showing who is sending email using their domain — legit or not.

climax.text: Google and Yahoo now require DMARC for bulk senders. No DMARC, no inbox.

punchline.text: DMARC enforces the rules SPF and DKIM set. Action, not just detection.

quiz.question: What does a DMARC policy of p=reject do?
options: Tells the receiver to block emails that fail authentication
Sends a warning to the sender
Logs the email but delivers it normally

details.summary: DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM by letting domain owners publish a policy for how receivers should handle email that fails authentication. A domain can instruct receivers to monitor, quarantine, or reject unauthenticated messages, providing the enforcement layer that SPF and DKIM lack alone.
details.whyItMatters: DMARC closes the gap between detection and action. Without it, SPF and DKIM can detect forgery but receivers have no guidance on what to do about it.
takeaways: DMARC publishes a policy for handling authentication failures
Policies range from monitoring to quarantine to reject
DMARC reports give domain owners visibility into abuse

faq.question: How do DMARC policies work?
faq.answer: The domain owner publishes a DMARC DNS record specifying a policy: none for monitoring, quarantine for spam folder, or reject for blocking. Receivers check SPF and DKIM results, verify alignment with the From domain, and apply the published policy to failures.

faq.question: What are DMARC reports?
faq.answer: Receivers send aggregate reports to the domain owner showing how many messages passed or failed authentication. These reports reveal unauthorized use of the domain, misconfigured legitimate senders, and the effectiveness of the authentication setup. They are essential for tuning policy.
